title: Facing the Press — The Economy
notebook: Unemployment remains above fifteen percent. The IMA conditions are still in effect.
The Krone has stabilized but has not recovered. Business confidence is fragile.
Nadia asks for a twelve-month plan and a guarantee the reforms will not cost us the recovery.
The press wants a number, a plan and a guarantee. I can give two of the three.

narrative.text: A reporter from the Kravenstal Worker stands — a heavyset man with ink-stained fingers and the particular directness of a regional journalist who has traveled four hours for this and intends to make the trip worthwhile.

Chancellor, the economic picture heading into Act Three is mixed at best. Unemployment remains above fifteen percent. The IMA conditions are still in effect. The Krone has stabilized but has not recovered. Business confidence is fragile. What is your economic plan for the next twelve months, and can you guarantee that the constitutional reforms will not come at the cost of the economic stability your government has fought to achieve?

The economy question. Everyone in this room knows the answer is complicated — the deficit is real, the IMA leash is real, the recovery is fragile and depends on decisions I have not yet made. But the press does not want complicated. They want a number, a plan, a guarantee. I can give them two of those three. The guarantee is the one I cannot honestly provide.

monologue: The economy question. Everyone knows the answer is complicated. The deficit is real, the IMA leash is real. The press wants a number, a plan, a guarantee. I can give them two of those three.

choices.text: "The economic plan is threefold. First: complete the IMA program on schedule — we are on track for quarter-three compliance. Second: the infrastructure investment fund begins disbursements next month, targeting Kravenstal and the northern provinces. Third: I am meeting with the business consortium next week to discuss the private investment framework. I cannot guarantee outcomes — no responsible leader can. What I can guarantee is that every economic decision this government makes will be transparent, documented, and subject to parliamentary review. That is new. That is what the constitution gives us."

reactions.text: He uncrosses his arms. The gesture is small but significant — it means the answer was adequate. Not brilliant. Adequate. In Vyktor's vocabulary, that is a passing grade.

choices.text: "I will not pretend the economic situation is good, because it is not. We inherited a deficit that the previous government concealed. The IMA conditions are painful but they are stabilizing the currency. What I will say is this: the economic plan is the same plan it has been since week one — fiscal discipline, targeted investment, and the hardest part, which is asking working Veltrians to accept short-term pain for long-term gain. I cannot guarantee that the pain will be short. I can guarantee that the gain will be real."

reactions.text: She writes something down. This time it is longer than a single line. When she looks up, there is something almost like approval in her expression — the particular approval of a journalist who has just been told the truth instead of a talking point. It is the most dangerous kind of approval, because it means she will quote you exactly, and exact quotes are harder to walk back than paraphrases.

choices.text: "The economic fundamentals are sound. The IMA program is proceeding on schedule. The infrastructure fund will create jobs. I am confident that the combination of fiscal discipline and targeted investment will produce results within the fiscal year. I am not going to make promises I cannot keep — that is what the previous government did, and it is how we arrived at the deficit we inherited."

reactions.text: Chancellor, you said 'fundamentals are sound.' The unemployment rate is sixteen percent. Which fundamentals are you referring to?
